chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad al-Jawhari from Sulayman ibn Dawud from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah from al-Zuhri from Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon them) said:

One day he said, "O Zuhri, from where have you come?" I said, "From the mosque." He said, "What were you discussing?" I said, "We were discussing the matter of fasting, and my opinion and the opinion of my companions converged that there is no obligatory fasting except the fasting of the month of Ramadan."

He said, "O Zuhri, it is not as you said. Fasting is of forty types: ten of them are obligatory like the obligation of the month of Ramadan; ten of them, their fasting is forbidden; fourteen of them, the owner has the choice: if he wishes he fasts and if he wishes he breaks the fast. And fasting of permission is of three types, and fasting of discipline, and fasting of permission (to break), and fasting of travel and illness."

I said, "May I be your ransom, so explain them to me." He said, "As for the obligatory: fasting of the month of Ramadan and two consecutive months in the expiation of Dhihar, due to the saying of Allah, Exalted and Mighty: 'And those who disavow their wives and then return to what they said, then a freeing of a slave before they touch each other. That is what you are admonished with, and Allah is Acquainted with what you do. So whoever does not find [a slave], then two consecutive months' fasting...'"
So whoever does not find [a slave], then two consecutive months' fasting

And fasting of two consecutive months for one who breaks a day of Ramadan, and fasting of two consecutive months in accidental killing for one who does not find the freedom of a slave is obligatory, due to the saying of Allah, Exalted and Mighty: 'And whoever kills a believer by mistake, then freeing of a believing slave and a compensation payment presented to the deceased's family...' until His saying: 'So whoever does not find [a slave], then two consecutive months' fasting, a repentance from Allah, and Allah is Knowing and Wise.'
So whoever does not find [a slave], then two consecutive months' fasting, a repentance from Allah, and Allah is Knowing and Wise

And fasting of three days in the expiation of an oath is obligatory. Allah, Exalted and Mighty, said: 'Then the expiation for your oaths is the feeding of ten needy people from the average of that which you feed your [family] or clothing them or the freeing of a slave. But whoever cannot find [then his expiation is] fasting for three days.' This is for one who does not find the means to feed. All of that is consecutive and not separate.
Then the expiation for your oaths is... fasting for three days

And fasting for the affliction of the throat/head is obligatory. Allah, Exalted and Mighty, said: 'So whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head [making him unable to fast] at the time of sacrifice, then an expiation of fasting or charity or sacrifice.' So the owner of this has the choice: if he wishes he fasts three [days].
So whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head... then an expiation of fasting or charity or sacrifice

And the fasting of the Dam of Tamattu' is obligatory for one who does not find the sacrifice. Allah, Exalted, said: 'So whoever performs Hajj or 'Umrah in his season, he must bring what he can find of sacrificial animals. So whoever does not find [then] fasting for three days during Hajj and seven when you have returned. Those are ten complete [days].'"
So whoever performs Tamattu'... then fasting for three days during Hajj and seven when you have returned. Those are ten complete [days]

And fasting of the compensation of game is obligatory. Allah, Exalted and Mighty, said: 'And whoever of you kills a game deliberately, his recompense is the equivalent of what he killed... or a compensation of feeding needy people or the equivalent of that in fasting.' Do you know how the equivalent of that becomes fasting, O Zuhri?" I said, "I do not know."
And whoever of you kills a game deliberately... or a compensation of feeding needy people or the equivalent of that in fasting

He said, "The game is appraised at a fair price, and that price is distributed in wheat, then that wheat is measured in sa' units, and he fasts one day for every half sa'. And fasting of the vow is obligatory, and fasting of the retreat (I'tikaf) is obligatory.

As for the forbidden fasting: fasting of the Day of Fitr, the Day of Adha, and three days of the Days of Tashriq. And fasting of the Day of Doubt: we were commanded to fast it and commanded not to fast it alone. We were commanded to fast it along with the fasting of Sha'ban, and we were commanded not to let a man fast it alone on the day people are doubtful about.

I said to him, "May I be your ransom, if he did not fast anything from Sha'ban, what should he do?" He said, "He intends on the night of Doubt that he is fasting from Sha'ban. If it turns out to be Ramadan, it will suffice for him, and if it is Sha'ban, it will not harm him."

I said, "And how does voluntary fasting suffice for an obligatory one?" He said, "If a man fasted a day of Ramadan and then learned [that it was Ramadan], it would suffice for him because the obligation fell upon that specific day."

And fasting of al-Wisal (fasting continuously without breaking) is forbidden, and fasting of al-Samt (fasting without speaking) is forbidden, and fasting of the vow of disobedience is forbidden, and fasting of the year-round (Dahr) is forbidden.

As for the fasting where the owner has the choice: fasting of Friday and Thursday, fasting of the White Days (13th, 14th, 15th), fasting of six days of Shawwal after Ramadan, fasting of the Day of Arafah and the Day of Ashura. All of that is such that the owner has the choice: if he wishes he fasts and if he wishes he breaks the fast.

As for fasting of permission: the woman does not fast voluntarily except with the permission of her husband, and the slave does not fast voluntarily except with the permission of his master, and the guest does not fast voluntarily except with the permission of his host. The Messenger of Allah (SAWW) said, "Whoever stays with a people, let him not fast voluntarily except with their permission."

As for fasting of discipline: the child is taken for fasting as discipline when he reaches maturity, and it is not obligatory. And likewise, one who breaks his fast due to an ailment from the beginning of the day, then becomes strong for the rest of the day, is commanded to abstain from food for the rest of the day as discipline, and it is not obligatory.

And likewise the traveler, if he ate from the beginning of the day then arrived home, is commanded to abstain for the rest of the day, and it is not obligatory. And likewise the menstruating woman, when she becomes pure, she abstains for the rest of her day.
As for fasting of permission (to break): whoever ate or drank forgetfully or vomited not deliberately, Allah, Exalted and Mighty, has permitted that for him, and his fasting suffices for him.

As for fasting of travel and illness: the general public have differed in this. Some said he fasts, others said he does not fast, and some said if he wishes he fasts and if he wishes he breaks the fast. As for us, we say he breaks the fast in both cases. If he fasts during travel or during illness, he must make up for it.
So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then an equal number of other days
This is the explanation of fasting."
ai.seo_question: What are the forty types of fasting in Shia jurisprudence and their respective rulings?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* presents a comprehensive taxonomy of fasting (*wujuh al-siyam*) attributed to Imam Ali ibn al-Husayn (AS), categorizing it into forty distinct types to clarify legal nuances often overlooked by the general public. It systematically distinguishes between obligatory fasts (such as Ramadan, *Kaffarat al-Zihar*, and *Kaffarat al-Yamin*), forbidden fasts (like *Sawm al-Visal*), and discretionary fasts, while specifically addressing the Shia ruling that travelers and the ill must fast if they choose to, with the obligation of making up the days later. The narration serves as a critical scholarly tool for understanding the interplay between Quranic exegesis and juristic deduction in Shia fiqh regarding expiations and conditional obligations.
